questions.prompt: What integration problem does MCP aim to solve?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: The N×M integration problem, where every AI application needs custom glue code for every tool or data source it connects to

Without a standard, every application-to-tool connection needs its own custom code, multiplying effort as both the number of applications and tools grow — MCP standardizes this into a common protocol both sides can implement once.
keyPoints: Without a standard, every application-to-tool connection needs its own custom code, multiplying effort as both the number of applications and tools grow — MCP standardizes this into a common protocol both sides can implement once.

questions.prompt: Does MCP change how an LLM decides which tool to call and with what arguments?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: No, the LLM's tool-calling mechanics stay exactly as covered in the LLM Engineering and Agents courses — MCP changes how tools get connected to the application

The model-facing mechanics of emitting a structured tool-call request and deciding which tool to use remain unchanged — MCP standardizes the integration and discovery layer beneath that, not the LLM's own decision process.
keyPoints: The model-facing mechanics of emitting a structured tool-call request and deciding which tool to use remain unchanged — MCP standardizes the integration and discovery layer beneath that, not the LLM's own decision process.

questions.prompt: How are MCP resources typically identified?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: By a URI-like scheme that lets a client refer to a specific resource unambiguously and lets a server organize resources in a structured way

A URI-like identification scheme provides structured, unambiguous references to resources, similar to how well-organized API endpoints use clear paths.
keyPoints: A URI-like identification scheme provides structured, unambiguous references to resources, similar to how well-organized API endpoints use clear paths.

questions.prompt: What mechanism does an HTTP-based MCP transport typically layer on top of ordinary HTTP requests?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: A streaming mechanism supporting an ongoing exchange of messages, similar in spirit to streaming LLM responses

Streaming support lets the server send a sequence of messages over time rather than being limited to one request-response pair, matching MCP's need for an ongoing message exchange.
keyPoints: Streaming support lets the server send a sequence of messages over time rather than being limited to one request-response pair, matching MCP's need for an ongoing message exchange.

questions.prompt: What information does a server return when a client lists its available tools?
questions.referenceAnswer: Tool listing returns exactly the kind of definition information (name, description, parameters) needed for the model to use the tool, just obtained dynamically rather than hardcoded.
keyPoints: Tool listing returns exactly the kind of definition information (name, description, parameters) needed for the model to use the tool, just obtained dynamically rather than hardcoded.

choices.text: Only the server's IP address
Each tool's name, description, and parameter schema — the same information a locally-defined tool would carry
The server's entire source code
A list of every other MCP server that exists

questions.prompt: Why might two different MCP servers exposing tools with the same name cause a problem?
questions.referenceAnswer: Without disambiguation, two similarly-named tools from different servers create ambiguity for both the model's selection and the application's routing — namespacing by server is a common fix.
keyPoints: Without disambiguation, two similarly-named tools from different servers create ambiguity for both the model's selection and the application's routing — namespacing by server is a common fix.

choices.text: This situation is technically impossible in MCP
The model and the orchestrating code need to be able to disambiguate which server's tool is meant, commonly handled via namespacing by server
Name collisions are automatically resolved by the JSON-RPC protocol
Only one MCP server can ever be connected at a time, so this never happens

questions.prompt: How can prompt injection occur through an MCP tool's result or a resource's content?
questions.referenceAnswer: Since the model has no inherent way to distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted data that merely looks like an instruction, malicious content returned via MCP can potentially manipulate the model's behavior.
keyPoints: Since the model has no inherent way to distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted data that merely looks like an instruction, malicious content returned via MCP can potentially manipulate the model's behavior.

choices.text: It's impossible for tool results or resources to contain any text at all
If the content contains text crafted to look like an instruction, and it's placed in the model's context like any observation, the model may follow it as if it were legitimate
Prompt injection can only happen through the initial user message, never through tool or resource content
MCP automatically strips all instructions from tool results and resources

questions.prompt: What extra diagnostic layer does an MCP-based system introduce compared to a purely locally-defined-tools setup?
questions.referenceAnswer: Since MCP servers are external code outside the host application's direct control, distinguishing application-level from server-level issues becomes a distinct diagnostic question that didn't exist the same way with purely local tools.
keyPoints: Since MCP servers are external code outside the host application's direct control, distinguishing application-level from server-level issues becomes a distinct diagnostic question that didn't exist the same way with purely local tools.

choices.text: No extra layer — MCP-based systems are diagnostically identical to locally-defined-tools setups
Whether an issue lives in the agent's own reasoning/routing, or in a connected MCP server's actual behavior — a layer outside the application's own control
MCP eliminates the need for any diagnostic layering at all
MCP-based systems cannot be diagnosed using any existing techniques

questions.prompt: A tool description asks an agent to send private data elsewhere. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Treat tool descriptions and returned content as untrusted input. Check user intent and resource authorization outside the model. Restrict destinations and credentials available to the tool.
keyPoints: Treat tool descriptions and returned content as untrusted input.
Check user intent and resource authorization outside the model.
Restrict destinations and credentials available to the tool.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Restrict destinations and credentials available to the tool. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Restrict destinations and credentials available to the tool.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Treat tool descriptions and returned content as untrusted input. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Treat tool descriptions and returned content as untrusted input.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.
